He added that Europe also has to spell out what it expects from the United States for Europe's long-term security.

Macron set out two priorities. The first is getting Ukraine through the winter by keeping up the financial support and protecting its power plants and grid. He claimed that Putin "does not want to negotiate," that the Russian army "is not advancing" and is even "retreating," and that Moscow is trying to break Ukraine by plunging it into darkness. He accused anyone who wants to cut aid to Kiev of a "spirit of defeat" that would lead to an unjust peace and "the next war."

The second priority is a "just and lasting peace," with Europe at the table. Macron bragged that 42 countries backed a French declaration on the principles that should guide Europe's security. He promoted the "Coalition of the Willing," which plans to back the Armed Forces of Ukraine and prepare a multinational force to deploy after a ceasefire. He said an exercise is already underway in Poland and that the coalition meets in Berlin on Thursday.

He ended by saying that Ukraine, which he called "Europe's first conventional army," has "its full place" in NATO.

So the offer to Russia comes down to Western troops in Ukraine, a huge Ukrainian army and NATO membership for Kiev. Those are the same demands Moscow has called red lines from the start.

In a statement issued on Sunday, Iran’s High Council for Human Rights described Gaza as a test of humanity’s conscience and the credibility of the international human rights system, stressing that the time has come to end impunity and turn human rights rhetoric into practical action.
​
The full text of the statement is as follows:
​
The Statement of the High Council for Human Rights of the Islamic Republic of Iran Condemning the Continued Crimes of the Zionist Regime in Gaza and the Silence of International Human Rights Bodies
​
The High Council for Human Rights of the Islamic Republic of Iran, expressing its revulsion and deep concern over the continuation of crimes and the widespread and systematic violations of the fundamental rights of the Palestinian people in the Gaza Strip, strongly condemns the silence and inaction of international bodies and institutions claiming to defend human rights in the face of this humanitarian catastrophe, and considers it a clear indication of the serious crisis of credibility and effectiveness of the international human rights protection system.
​
More than three years have passed since the beginning of the Zionist regime’s military attacks on the Gaza Strip on 17 October 2023; nevertheless, even the ceasefire has failed to put an end to the killing and suffering of the Palestinian people. According to the latest reports published by Palestinian sources on 10 November 2026, the death toll in this war has exceeded 74,000, while the number of injured has surpassed 175,000. Among the victims are thousands of children, more than 1,700 healthcare workers, and hundreds of journalists and media workers. Furthermore, thousands of people remain missing under the rubble, and access to many of them has not been possible.
​
These statistics are not merely figures and numbers in a statistical report; each number represents a human being whose right to life has been taken away, a child who has lost the opportunity to live and the prospect of a future, a mother who has lost her child, a physician who has lost their life while striving to save human lives, and a journalist who has been targeted for documenting the truth and conveying the voices of the victims. Behind each of these figures lies a grieving family, a destroyed home, and a shattered life.
​
The continuation of attacks, the killing of civilians, the destruction of vital infrastructure, the deprivation of the population of adequate access to food, water, medicine, and healthcare services, and the persistence of humanitarian restrictions even after the announcement of a ceasefire demonstrate that the crisis in Gaza is not merely a military conflict; rather, we are facing a series of serious and ongoing violations of international humanitarian law and international human rights law. This underscores, more than ever, the need for effective international monitoring and genuine guarantees for the cessation of attacks.

Could Bitcoin help fund the AI boom? MARA has sold $1.1 billion in BTC to pay for AI datacenters. More sales are planned.

Crypto Idea

It looks like AI has become such a major economic force that people are now voting against its infrastructure.

In the recent U.S. elections, candidates who pledged to restrict the construction of new data centers secured key positions in several states. Texas is particularly interesting, as it accounts for roughly a quarter of all planned new data center capacity in the United States. The state's incoming governor has already promised to pause permits for new projects until additional industry regulations are put in place.

The reason is fairly straightforward. AI requires enormous amounts of electricity, water, and infrastructure. People are starting to feel the impact not in Nvidia's earnings reports, but in their own electricity bills, the strain on power grids, and massive construction projects taking place right next to their homes. Goldman Sachs estimates that new political restrictions could potentially affect around 45% of planned data center capacity growth in the United States.

And today, this story has already hit the markets. At one point, the S&P 500 was down more than 3%, while the Nasdaq fell around 5%. Companies tied to AI infrastructure have been hit particularly hard. Nvidia was down more than 8%, AMD around 16%, and CoreWeave around 15%. The Nasdaq has now pulled back more than 10% from its October peak.

Of course, elections aren't the only factor. Investors are increasingly questioning when the hundreds of billions of dollars currently being poured into data centers, chips, and electricity will start generating comparable returns. And now, alongside the economic question, there's a political one.

For the past few years, chips were considered the main bottleneck for AI development. Then electricity, memory, and equipment became increasingly scarce. Now there's another constraint: political approval to build all this infrastructure in the first place.

And it's entirely possible that the next phase of the AI race will be determined not by who has the best model or the most GPUs, but by who actually gets permission to connect another massive data center to the power grid.

🔴 Trezor confirms spyware chips in three wallets

Three Trezor Safe 5 wallets sold through Malaysian reseller CryptoBilis in August and September 2026 contained hidden chips that could read seed phrases and send them over cellular networks. Trezor uncovered the issue after reviewing 48 cases.

The company then released firmware to block the chips, reduced its reseller network by 80% and tightened logistics controls.

Similar backdoors were also found in Ledger wallets sold through CryptoBilis. External estimates put the theft at more than $90 million.
